title: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts

learn.hook: Two college friends in Pune start a cloud-kitchen and split the profit 50:50. Without signing anything formal, they may already be partners in the eyes of the law!
points: Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.
Essential features: two or more persons, an agreement (oral or written), a lawful business, sharing of profits, and mutual agency (each partner is both an agent and a principal).
Liability of partners is unlimited: if the firm's assets fall short, partners' private assets can be used to pay the firm's debts. Partners are jointly and severally liable.
Minimum 2 partners; the maximum is 50 under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014.
Accounts special to partnership: partners' capital (and current) accounts, the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, and adjustments when the firm is reconstituted.

example.q: Meera and Kabir jointly inherit a flat in Jaipur and share the rent they get from it. Are they partners?
steps: Check each feature: two persons – yes; sharing of returns – yes.
But there is no agreement to carry on a business; they merely co-own property.
Sharing income from jointly owned property does not by itself create a partnership.
example.answer: No. Co-owners sharing rent are not partners, because there is no agreement to carry on a business together.

learn.reallife: Many Indian CA firms, law chambers and family-run kirana wholesalers in Chandni Chowk work as partnership firms because partnership is quick to form and needs no heavy legal process.

games.title: Partnership facts
items: A partnership can be formed by an oral agreement.
The Act needs an agreement; it may be oral or written, though written is wiser.
A partnership firm can have just one partner.
At least two persons are needed to form a partnership.
The maximum number of partners allowed is 50.
The Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 cap partners at 50.
Registration of a partnership firm is compulsory under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
Registration is optional, though an unregistered firm faces some legal disadvantages.
A partner's liability for the firm's debts is limited to his capital.
Liability of partners is unlimited.
Partnership accounts need a Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
It shows how the firm's profit is distributed among partners.

quiz.q: Which section of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines 'partnership'?
quiz.explain: Section 4 gives the definition. Section 13 covers rights such as interest on loans, and Section 48 deals with settlement on dissolution.
steps: The definition of partnership is in Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
Section 13 covers rights like loan interest; Section 48 covers settlement on dissolution.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the definition section with other well-known sections of the Act

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of partners a partnership firm can have under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014?
quiz.explain: Rule 10 of the 2014 Rules prescribes a maximum of 50 partners.
steps: The Companies Act, 2013 lets the government prescribe a limit.
Rule 10 of the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 fixes the maximum at 50 partners.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the older limits of 10/20 or the Companies Act upper ceiling of 100

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an essential feature of a partnership?
options: Sharing of profits of a business
quiz.explain: Registration is optional under the Act. Agreement, business, profit sharing and mutual agency are essential.
steps: Essential features: two or more persons, agreement, lawful business, sharing of profits, mutual agency.
Registration of a firm is optional under the Act.
So compulsory registration is NOT an essential feature.
Answer: Compulsory registration of the firm
quiz.mistake: Thinks registration is a condition for a partnership to exist

quiz.q: 'Mutual agency' in a partnership means that:
options: each partner must contribute equal capital
the firm is an agent of its customers
only the senior partner can bind the firm
each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners, and also a principal
quiz.explain: Every partner can bind the firm by acts done in the ordinary course of business and is, in turn, bound by the acts of others.
steps: Mutual agency: every partner can bind the firm by acts in the ordinary course of business.
Each partner is also bound by the acts of the others, so each is both agent and principal.
Answer: each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners, and also a principal
quiz.mistake: Confuses mutual agency with equal capital or with a single managing partner

quiz.q: A firm's assets are ₹6,00,000 and its outside liabilities are ₹9,00,000. What happens to the shortfall?
options: Partners must pay it from their private assets, as their liability is unlimited
Only the partner with the highest capital pays it
The firm is converted into a company
quiz.explain: Partners are jointly and severally liable without limit, so creditors can recover the ₹3,00,000 shortfall from partners' personal assets.
steps: Partners' liability is unlimited, joint and several.
So creditors can recover ₹3,00,000 from partners' private assets.
Answer: Partners must pay it from their private assets, as their liability is unlimited
quiz.mistake: Treats a partnership like a company with limited liability

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two people who jointly own a godown and share its rent are not partners.
Reason (R): A partnership arises only from an agreement to carry on a business and share its profits.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Co-owning property and sharing its rent is not carrying on a business by agreement, which is exactly what R states.
steps: A: co-owners sharing a godown's rent are not partners – true.
R: partnership arises only from an agreement to carry on a business and share profits – true.
Co-owning is not carrying on a business, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Assumes any sharing of income creates a partnership

quiz.q: Which pair of accounts is special to partnership firms and not needed by a sole proprietor?
options: Partners' current accounts and the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
quiz.explain: A sole trader takes the whole profit, so there is no appropriation among owners. Partners need appropriation and separate capital/current accounts.
steps: A sole trader keeps the whole profit, so nothing is appropriated among owners.
Partners need the P&L Appropriation Account and separate current (or capital) accounts.
Answer: Partners' current accounts and the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
quiz.mistake: Lists general accounting records common to all businesses

quiz.q: Which minimum number of persons is needed to form a partnership?
quiz.explain: Partnership is a relation between persons, so at least two are needed. Seven is the minimum for a public company.
steps: Partnership is a relation between persons, so at least two are needed.
Seven is the minimum for a public company, not a firm.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up partnership with the minimum membership of a public company

teach.ask: Gappu thinks any two people who share money are partners. Explain the essential features of a partnership.
teach.praise: Perfect! Agreement, business, profit sharing and mutual agency – now Gappu knows a partnership when he sees one.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: is it just sharing money, or must there be an agreement to run a business with each partner acting as agent?

revise.summary: Partnership (Section 4) is the relation between persons who agree to share profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. It needs 2 to 50 persons, an agreement, a business, profit sharing and mutual agency, with unlimited liability.
focus: The Section 4 definition and the five essential features
Why co-owners are not partners
Unlimited, joint and several liability
Accounts special to partnership firms
remember: Section 4, Indian Partnership Act, 1932
Minimum 2, maximum 50 partners (Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014)
Mutual agency: each partner is agent and principal
traps: Registration is not an essential feature
Co-owners sharing rent are not partners
Partners' liability is unlimited, not limited to capital

topics.title: Partnership deed and rules when there is no deed

learn.hook: Friends fall out over money more often than over cricket. A partnership deed is the rulebook that prevents the fight before it begins.
points: A partnership deed is the written agreement among partners, ideally stamped as per the Indian Stamp Act. It usually states the firm's name, capital of each partner, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salary/commission, rules for admission, retirement and dissolution, and how accounts are kept.
If there is no deed (or the deed is silent), the Act applies: profits and losses are shared equally.
No deed: no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, and no salary or commission to any partner.
No deed: a partner's loan to the firm earns interest at 6% p.a. (Section 13).
Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Account, so it is allowed even if the firm makes a loss. It is not an appropriation.

example.q: Asha and Vikram have no deed. Asha's capital is ₹5,00,000 and Vikram's ₹3,00,000. Vikram also lent the firm ₹1,00,000 on 1 April 2025. Profit for 2025-26 before any interest is ₹86,000. Divide the profit.
steps: No deed → no interest on capital; partners share equally.
Vikram's loan gets 6% p.a.: ₹1,00,000 × 6% = ₹6,000, charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
example.answer: Interest on loan to Vikram ₹6,000; profit share ₹40,000 each.

learn.reallife: Many CA firms, clinics and family businesses in Bengaluru run as partnership firms, and the partners' first legal document is the deed that spells out who gets what.

games.title: Deed is silent: allowed or not?

items.text: In the absence of a deed, interest on a partner's loan is allowed at ___ per annum.
In the absence of a deed, profits are shared ___.
Interest on a partner's loan is debited to the ___ Account.
The deed is a ___ document signed by all partners.

quiz.q: In the absence of a partnership deed, partners share profits and losses:
options: in the ratio of their capitals
in the ratio of time devoted
as decided by the senior partner
quiz.explain: The Act lays down equal sharing whenever the deed is absent or silent.
steps: When there is no deed (or it is silent), the Act applies.
The Act says profits and losses are shared equally.
quiz.mistake: Assumes capital contributed decides the share

quiz.q: Rate of interest allowed on a partner's loan when there is no deed:
quiz.explain: Section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act provides 6% per annum on loans and advances by partners.
steps: Section 13 of the Act gives interest on a partner's loan at 6% p.a. when there is no agreement.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the interest on calls in arrears/advance used for companies

quiz.q: Karan, a partner, lent ₹50,000 to the firm on 1 October 2025. The firm has no deed and closes books on 31 March 2026. Interest on his loan for the year is:
quiz.explain: The loan was used for 6 months: ₹50,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,500.
quiz.mistake: Charges a full year's interest instead of interest for 6 months

quiz.q: Interest on a partner's loan is treated as:
options: an appropriation, debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
a reduction in the partner's capital
an item credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
a charge against profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Account
quiz.explain: A loan makes the partner a lender too; interest on it is an expense of the firm, payable even if there is a loss.
steps: A partner's loan makes him a lender to the firm.
Interest on it is an expense (a charge against profit), not an appropriation.
So it is debited to the Profit and Loss Account and paid even in a loss.
Answer: a charge against profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Account
quiz.mistake: Treats every amount paid to a partner as an appropriation of profit

quiz.q: Riya works full-time in the firm while her partner Dev works only on weekends. There is no deed. Riya claims a salary of ₹20,000 per month. Is she entitled to it?
options: No, a partner gets no salary unless the deed or partners' agreement provides it
Yes, but only at half the rate
Only if the firm earns more than ₹5,00,000
quiz.explain: Without a deed, no partner is entitled to salary or commission, however much time is devoted.
steps: No deed → no salary or commission to any partner.
Working full-time does not change this rule.
So Riya is not entitled to the salary.
Answer: No, a partner gets no salary unless the deed or partners' agreement provides it
quiz.mistake: Thinks extra effort automatically earns remuneration

quiz.q: Rohan's capital is ₹4,00,000 and Simran's is ₹2,00,000. There is no deed. The firm's profit is ₹90,000 and there are no loans. Simran's share of profit is:
quiz.explain: With no deed, profit is shared equally regardless of capital: ₹90,000 ÷ 2 = ₹45,000.
quiz.mistake: Shares profit in the capital ratio 2:1

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Interest on a partner's loan is paid even if the firm suffers a loss.
Reason (R): Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: Because it is a charge (an expense), it must be paid whether there is profit or loss.
steps: A: interest on a partner's loan is paid even in a loss – true.
R: it is a charge against profit – true.
Being a charge (expense) is exactly why it is paid in a loss.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats loan interest like interest on capital, which needs profits

quiz.q: Which of these does a partnership deed usually NOT contain?
options: Rate of interest on capital and drawings
Rules for admission and retirement of partners
The personal income-tax return of each partner
quiz.explain: A deed records the terms of the partnership among partners, not their personal tax filings.
steps: A deed records terms among partners: ratio, interest, salary, admission and retirement rules.
A partner's personal income-tax return is not part of it.
Answer: The personal income-tax return of each partner
quiz.mistake: Thinks the deed records all personal finances of partners

teach.ask: Gappu's firm has no deed. Tell him what the law says about sharing profit, interest and salary.
teach.praise: Spot on! Equal sharing, no interest on capital or drawings, no salary, and 6% on loans – Gappu has the rulebook.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what rate does a partner earn on a loan given to the firm when there is no deed?

revise.summary: A partnership deed records the terms of partnership. If there is no deed, profits are shared equally, there is no interest on capital or drawings, no salary or commission, and interest on a partner's loan is 6% p.a., charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
focus: Contents of a partnership deed
The rules that apply when there is no deed
Treating interest on a partner's loan as a charge
remember: No deed: equal sharing; no interest on capital or drawings; no salary or commission
Interest on partner's loan: 6% p.a. (Section 13), debited to P&L A/c
traps: Don't give interest on capital or salary when there is no deed
Interest on a partner's loan is a charge, not an appropriation
Don't share profits in capital ratio when the deed is absent

learn.hook: Two accounts or one? The choice decides whether a partner's capital looks rock-steady like Mount Abu or bobs up and down like a boat on the Ganga.
points: Fixed capital method: each partner has a Capital Account and a Current Account. The capital account changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn.
Under the fixed method, interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit, drawings and interest on drawings go to the Current Account.
Fluctuating capital method: only one Capital Account per partner; all these adjustments are recorded in it, so its balance keeps changing.
A fixed capital account always shows a credit balance; a current account (or a fluctuating capital account) can show a debit balance.
If the question does not say which method to use, prepare fluctuating capital accounts.

example.q: Under fixed capitals, Nisha's capital is ₹5,00,000 and her current account opens with ₹20,000 Cr. During the year: interest on capital ₹50,000, salary ₹30,000, profit share ₹60,000, drawings ₹40,000, interest on drawings ₹2,000. Find her closing balances.

learn.reallife: Big Indian partnership firms like audit firms often fix each partner's capital and run a current account, so the stake stays clear while yearly earnings flow separately.

games.title: Fixed capital method: which account?

Permanent withdrawal of capital
Opening capital contributed

games.title: Capital method check
items: Under the fixed capital method, a capital account can show a debit balance.
A fixed capital account always shows a credit balance; only the current account may turn debit.
Under the fluctuating method, drawings are debited to the capital account.
There is only one account, so all adjustments go there.
When the method is not stated, capital accounts are prepared as fluctuating.
That is the standard assumption in examinations.
Under the fixed method, share of profit is credited to the capital account.
It is credited to the current account.
A debit balance of a partner's current account is shown on the assets side of the balance sheet.
It means the partner owes the firm.
The fluctuating method needs two accounts for each partner.
It needs only one account, the capital account.

quiz.q: Under the fixed capital method, which item is recorded in the partner's Capital Account?
quiz.explain: Only permanent changes in capital, such as introducing or withdrawing capital, touch the fixed capital account.
steps: Under the fixed method, the capital account changes only for permanent changes in capital.
Interest on capital, drawings and profit share go to the current account.
So additional capital introduced goes to the Capital Account.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every partner-related item goes to the capital account

quiz.q: Nisha's current account (fixed capital method) opens at ₹20,000 Cr. Interest on capital ₹50,000, salary ₹30,000, profit share ₹60,000, drawings ₹40,000 and interest on drawings ₹2,000. Closing current account balance:
quiz.explain: Credits total ₹1,60,000 and debits ₹42,000, so the balance is ₹1,18,000 Cr.
quiz.mistake: Adds interest on drawings instead of deducting it

quiz.q: Under the fluctuating method, Arjun's opening capital is ₹3,00,000. Interest on capital ₹18,000, salary ₹24,000, profit share ₹40,000, drawings ₹30,000, interest on drawings ₹1,500. Closing capital:
quiz.mistake: Adds interest on drawings as if it were income for the partner

quiz.q: Under the fixed capital method, which account of a partner may show a debit balance?
quiz.explain: Heavy drawings or losses can make the current account debit, while the fixed capital account stays credit.
steps: The fixed capital account always shows a credit balance.
Heavy drawings or losses can make the current account debit.
So the Current Account may show a debit balance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the fixed capital account absorbs losses and drawings

quiz.q: A question gives partners' capitals but does not say whether they are fixed or fluctuating. You should prepare:
options: a joint capital account for all partners
quiz.explain: When no method is given, the fluctuating capital method is followed.
steps: Rule: if the method is not stated, use the fluctuating capital method.
quiz.mistake: Assumes fixed capitals are the default

quiz.q: Where is a debit balance in a partner's current account shown in the firm's balance sheet?
options: It is deducted from the firm's profit
It is not shown at all
quiz.explain: A debit balance means the partner owes money to the firm, so it is an asset of the firm.
steps: A debit balance in a current account means the partner owes the firm money.
Money owed to the firm is an asset.
So it is shown on the assets side.
quiz.mistake: Puts every partner-related balance on the liabilities side

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Under the fixed capital method, a partner's drawings are debited to the current account.
Reason (R): Under this method, the capital account changes only when capital is introduced or withdrawn permanently.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Since the capital account is kept fixed, regular drawings must go elsewhere – the current account.
steps: A: drawings are debited to the current account under the fixed method – true.
R: the capital account changes only for permanent capital changes – true.
Since capital is kept fixed, drawings must go to the current account.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to link why the current account exists

quiz.q: Fixed capital method: Meena's capital is ₹4,00,000; her current account opens at ₹10,000 Dr. During the year she gets interest on capital ₹32,000 and a profit share of ₹48,000; her drawings are ₹50,000. Her closing current account balance (credit) is:
quiz.explain: Start at −10,000, add 32,000 and 48,000, subtract 50,000: the result is +20,000, a credit balance.
quiz.mistake: Treats the opening debit balance as a credit

teach.ask: Gappu cannot tell fixed capital from fluctuating capital. Explain the difference.
teach.praise: Great! Fixed = capital plus current account; fluctuating = one capital account that takes every adjustment.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: under the fixed method, where do drawings and profit share go?

revise.summary: Under the fixed capital method each partner has a capital account (changed only by permanent additions or withdrawals) and a current account for interest, salary, profit and drawings. Under the fluctuating method, all items go to one capital account.
focus: Which items go to the capital account and which to the current account
Which balances can be debit
Default method when not stated
Showing a debit current account in the balance sheet
remember: Fixed method: capital account + current account
Fluctuating method: one capital account for all items
Method not stated → fluctuating capital accounts
Debit current balance → assets side
traps: Don't record drawings or profit share in a fixed capital account
A fixed capital account always has a credit balance
A debit current account is an asset, not a liability

learn.hook: The firm has made its profit. Now comes the IPL-auction moment – who gets what, in which order?
points: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is an extension of the Profit and Loss Account. It starts with net profit and shows how it is distributed among partners.
Debit side: interest on capital, salary/commission to partners, transfer to reserve, and finally each partner's share of profit. Credit side: net profit (b/d) and interest on drawings.
Commission as a % of net profit before charging it = NP × rate/100. After charging it = NP × rate/(100 + rate).
Transfer to reserve is an appropriation; the remaining profit is then divided in the profit-sharing ratio.
Entry for appropriation items: Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c, Cr Partners' Capital (or Current) A/cs; for interest on drawings: Dr Partners' Capital/Current A/cs, Cr P&L Appropriation A/c.

example.q: Net profit ₹4,00,000. Interest on capital: A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000. Salary to B ₹50,000. Interest on drawings: A ₹4,000, B ₹6,000. Transfer to reserve ₹40,000. A and B share 3:2. Find each share of profit.

learn.reallife: A family-run sweets firm in Kolkata may pay the partner who runs the shop floor a salary first, put some profit aside as reserve before Durga Puja, and share the rest.

games.title: P&L Appropriation: debit or credit side?
items: Interest on capital
Salary to a partner
Commission to a partner
Transfer to general reserve
Net profit b/d
Interest on drawings

items.text: Commission of 10% on net profit after charging it, when profit before commission is ₹2,20,000, is ₹___.
Commission of 5% on profit before charging it, on ₹2,00,000, is ₹___.
Interest on drawings is shown on the ___ side of the appropriation account.
Interest on a partner's loan is shown in the ___ Account, not the appropriation account.

quiz.q: Which of these is debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?
options: Rent paid to a partner for using his shop
quiz.explain: Partners' salary is an appropriation. Loan interest and rent to a partner are charges in the Profit and Loss Account; interest on drawings is credited.
steps: Debit side of the appropriation account: interest on capital, partners' salary or commission, transfer to reserve, profit shares.
Loan interest and rent to a partner are charges in the P&L Account; interest on drawings is credited.
So salary to a partner is debited.
quiz.mistake: Treats every payment to a partner as an appropriation

quiz.q: Profit before commission is ₹2,10,000. The manager-partner gets 5% commission on net profit after charging such commission. Commission =
quiz.explain: After-charging commission = 2,10,000 × 5/105 = ₹10,000; then 2,00,000 × 5% = 10,000 checks out.
quiz.mistake: Calculates 5% on the profit before commission

quiz.q: Same firm: profit before commission ₹2,10,000, but now commission is 5% of net profit before charging it. Commission =
quiz.explain: Before-charging commission is simply 5% of ₹2,10,000 = ₹10,500.
steps: Given: profit before commission ₹2,10,000; commission 5% of net profit before charging it.
quiz.mistake: Uses the after-charging formula when it is not asked

quiz.q: Net profit ₹4,00,000; interest on capital A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000; salary B ₹50,000; interest on drawings A ₹4,000, B ₹6,000; reserve ₹40,000. A and B share 3:2. B's share of profit:
steps: Credit side: net profit 4,00,000 + interest on drawings (4,000 + 6,000) = 4,10,000
Debits before sharing: interest on capital (30,000 + 20,000) + salary 50,000 + reserve 40,000 = 1,40,000
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add interest on drawings to the profit

quiz.q: How is interest on drawings recorded?
options: Dr Partner's Capital/Current A/c / Cr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c
Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c / Cr Partner's Capital A/c
Dr Profit and Loss A/c / Cr Partner's Capital A/c
Dr Drawings A/c / Cr Cash A/c
quiz.explain: Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm and a burden on the partner, so the partner is debited and the appropriation account credited.
steps: Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm and a burden on the partner.
So debit the partner's capital or current account and credit the P&L Appropriation Account.
Answer: Dr Partner's Capital/Current A/c / Cr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c
quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry, treating it like interest on capital

quiz.q: A, B and C share profits equally. C gets a salary of ₹2,000 per month. Net profit is ₹1,20,000. A's share of profit:
quiz.explain: Salary for the year = ₹24,000; divisible profit ₹96,000 ÷ 3 = ₹32,000.
quiz.mistake: Divides the full profit without deducting the yearly salary

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Salary to a partner is credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
Reason (R): Salary to a partner is an appropriation of profit.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are false
quiz.explain: Salary is an appropriation (R true), so it is debited – not credited – to the appropriation account (A false).
steps: R: salary to a partner is an appropriation of profit – true.
Appropriations are debited, not credited, to the appropriation account, so A is false.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Confuses the side on which appropriations appear

quiz.q: Net profit ₹1,50,000. 10% of net profit is transferred to general reserve and the rest is shared by X and Y in 2:1. X's share:
quiz.mistake: Shares the profit before transferring to reserve

teach.ask: Gappu has a net profit figure and no idea how to split it. Walk him through the appropriation account.
teach.praise: Brilliant! Interest, salary or commission, reserve, then the balance in the ratio – Gappu's profit is properly shared.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: before splitting the balance in the ratio, what has to be deducted first?

revise.summary: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account starts with net profit, adds interest on drawings, and deducts interest on capital, partners' salary or commission and transfer to reserve. The balance is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
focus: Items on each side of the appropriation account
Commission before vs after charging it
Journal entries for appropriation items and interest on drawings
remember: Debit: interest on capital, salary, commission, transfer to reserve, profit shares
Credit: net profit, interest on drawings
Commission before charging = NP × rate/100; after charging = NP × rate/(100 + rate)
traps: Salary to a partner is debited, not credited
Interest on a partner's loan belongs in the P&L Account, not the appropriation account
Use rate/(100 + rate) only when commission is on profit after charging it

learn.hook: Money parked in a fixed deposit earns interest. Money parked in your firm deserves a reward too – if the deed says so.
points: Interest on capital is allowed only if the deed provides it. It is calculated on the opening capital for the year.
Additional capital introduced during the year earns interest from the date of introduction; capital withdrawn stops earning interest from the date of withdrawal.
Unless the deed treats it as a charge, interest on capital is an appropriation, so it is allowed only out of profits. If the firm makes a loss, no interest on capital is allowed.
If the profit is less than the total interest on capital, the available profit is divided in the ratio of interest on capital of each partner.
Working back: Opening capital = Closing capital − profit share credited − additional capital + drawings + losses debited (before interest on capital).

example.q: Anil's capital on 1 April 2025 is ₹4,00,000. He adds ₹1,00,000 on 1 October 2025. Interest on capital is 10% p.a. Find interest for the year ending 31 March 2026.

learn.reallife: An RBI repo-rate change ripples into FD rates, and firms often link the interest-on-capital rate in their deed to such market rates.

items.q: ₹2,00,000 at 10% p.a. for a full year
₹3,00,000 at 6% p.a. for a full year
₹1,20,000 added on 1 Jan, 10% p.a., year ends 31 Mar
₹60,000 withdrawn on 1 Oct, 10% p.a.: interest lost
₹2,50,000 at 12% p.a. for a full year

games.title: Interest on capital rules
items: Interest on capital is allowed when the firm has a loss, if it is an appropriation.
Being an appropriation, it needs profits.
If profit is short of total interest on capital, profit is divided in the ratio of interest.
That is the rule when interest is payable only out of profits.
Additional capital earns interest from the date it is introduced.
Interest is on a time basis.
Interest on capital is allowed at 6% even if there is no deed.
Without a deed, no interest on capital is allowed; 6% applies to loans.
Interest on capital is credited to the partner's capital or current account.
The appropriation account is debited and the partner credited.

quiz.q: Opening capital ₹4,00,000; additional capital ₹1,00,000 on 1 October; interest 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Interest on capital:
quiz.explain: ₹40,000 on opening capital plus ₹5,000 on the addition for 6 months.
quiz.mistake: Charges interest on the addition for the full year

quiz.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000; ₹50,000 withdrawn on 1 January; interest 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Interest on capital:
quiz.explain: Interest on ₹3,00,000 for 12 months is ₹30,000, minus interest on ₹50,000 for the 3 months after withdrawal (₹1,250).
quiz.mistake: Deducts the withdrawal for the whole year

quiz.q: Interest on capital: A ₹30,000 and B ₹20,000. The deed allows interest only out of profits. Profit is ₹40,000. B will get interest of:
quiz.explain: Profit is short, so ₹40,000 is shared in the ratio of interest 3:2. B gets 2/5 × 40,000 = ₹16,000.
quiz.mistake: Shares the available profit equally

quiz.q: The deed provides interest on capital at 10% as an appropriation. The firm makes a loss of ₹25,000. Interest on capital allowed:
quiz.explain: As an appropriation, interest on capital needs profits; with a loss, nothing is allowed.
steps: The deed treats interest on capital as an appropriation.
An appropriation needs profit; the firm has a loss of ₹25,000.
So no interest on capital is allowed.
quiz.mistake: Treats interest on capital as a fixed charge like loan interest

quiz.q: Ravi's closing capital (before interest on capital) is ₹5,40,000. During the year his profit share was ₹80,000, drawings ₹60,000 and additional capital ₹40,000 (introduced on day 1 of the year). His opening capital was:
quiz.explain: Reverse the year: remove the profit share and the additional capital, and add back the drawings.
quiz.mistake: Adds the profit share and deducts the drawings, moving forward instead of backward

quiz.q: X's capital is ₹6,00,000 and Y's ₹4,00,000. Interest on capital is 5% p.a. Profit is ₹75,000, shared equally after interest. X's total (interest + share):
quiz.explain: X's interest ₹30,000; Y's ₹20,000. Balance ₹25,000 shared equally, so X gets ₹12,500 more.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the interest to X's profit share

quiz.q: When the profit is less than the total interest on capital (interest payable only out of profit), the profit is divided in the ratio of:
options: capitals at the end of the year
interest on capital due to each partner
quiz.explain: The available profit is shared in proportion to the interest each partner would have received.
steps: Profit is less than total interest on capital, and interest is payable only out of profit.
So the available profit is divided in the ratio of interest on capital due to each partner.
Answer: interest on capital due to each partner
quiz.mistake: Uses the profit-sharing ratio by habit

quiz.q: Interest on capital is normally calculated on:
options: closing capital for the full year
opening capital, adjusted for capital added or withdrawn on a time basis
quiz.explain: Closing capital already includes the year's profit; interest is on capital actually used during the year.
steps: Closing capital already includes the year's profit, so it is not used.
Interest is on opening capital, adjusted for capital added or withdrawn for the time used.
Answer: opening capital, adjusted for capital added or withdrawn on a time basis
quiz.mistake: Uses closing capital, which already includes the current year's profit

teach.ask: Gappu wants to calculate interest on capital. Tell him the rules.
teach.praise: Super! Opening capital, time basis for changes, nothing in a loss, and the ratio of interest when profits fall short.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what if the profit is smaller than the total interest on capital?

revise.summary: Interest on capital is allowed only if the deed provides it, on opening capital adjusted for additions and withdrawals by time. As an appropriation it needs profit: none in a loss, and profit shared in the ratio of interest if profit is insufficient.
focus: Calculating interest on opening and additional capital for the right months
No interest on capital in a loss
Sharing insufficient profit in the ratio of interest
remember: Interest on capital = capital × rate × months/12
Appropriation → allowed only out of profits
Profit < interest → share profit in ratio of interest due
traps: Don't calculate interest on closing capital
Don't allow interest on capital (as appropriation) when there is a loss
Additional capital earns interest only from the date it is introduced

learn.hook: Taking money out of the firm for your sister's wedding shopping? The firm may charge you interest – and the date you withdraw matters.
points: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed provides it. It is calculated for the time the money stays out of the business, up to the end of the year.
Different amounts on different dates: use the product method – multiply each amount by the months remaining, add the products, then interest = total products × rate/100 × 1/12.
Equal monthly drawings for a full year: average period 6.5 months (beginning of each month), 6 months (middle) and 5.5 months (end).
Equal quarterly drawings for a full year: average period 7.5 months (beginning of each quarter), 6 months (middle) and 4.5 months (end).
Dates not given: charge for 6 months on the total. If a flat rate is given (not 'per annum'), time is ignored.

example.q: Partner Leela withdrew ₹10,000 on 1 July, ₹20,000 on 1 October and ₹15,000 on 1 January. The year ends on 31 March; interest is 6% p.a. Find interest on drawings.

learn.reallife: Just as a bank charges interest from the day a credit-card amount is spent, a firm charges interest on drawings from the day money is withdrawn.

games.title: Timing of equal drawings ↔ average months

items.q: ₹60,000 drawn in total, dates unknown, 10% p.a.
₹5,000 at the start of every month, 12% p.a.
₹5,000 at the end of every month, 12% p.a.
₹20,000 at the start of each quarter, 10% p.a.
₹20,000 at the end of each quarter, 10% p.a.

quiz.q: Drawings: ₹10,000 on 1 July, ₹20,000 on 1 October, ₹15,000 on 1 January. Year ends 31 March. Rate 6% p.a. Interest on drawings:
quiz.mistake: Charges interest on all drawings for the full year

quiz.q: A partner draws ₹5,000 at the beginning of every month for the year. Interest is 10% p.a. Interest on drawings:
quiz.explain: Beginning of each month → average 6.5 months on ₹60,000: 60,000 × 10% × 6.5/12 = ₹3,250.
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 months, the average for middle-of-month drawings

quiz.q: For equal drawings at the END of every month for a full year, interest is charged for an average period (in months) of:
quiz.explain: The first drawing stays out for 11 months and the last for 0; the average is 5.5 months.
steps: Equal monthly drawings at the end of each month.
The first stays out 11 months, the last 0 months.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up end-of-month with beginning-of-month timing

quiz.q: A partner draws ₹30,000 at the beginning of each quarter. Interest is 8% p.a. Interest on drawings for the year:
quiz.explain: Total ₹1,20,000; beginning of quarter → average 7.5 months: 1,20,000 × 8% × 7.5/12 = ₹6,000.
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 months instead of 7.5

quiz.q: A partner draws ₹30,000 at the end of each quarter. Interest is 8% p.a. Interest on drawings:
quiz.explain: End of quarter → average 4.5 months: 1,20,000 × 8% × 4.5/12 = ₹3,600.
steps: Given: ₹30,000 at the end of each quarter; 8% p.a.
Total drawings = 4 × ₹30,000 = ₹1,20,000; end of quarter → average 4.5 months.
quiz.mistake: Uses the beginning-of-quarter average of 7.5 months

quiz.q: Total drawings of a partner are ₹48,000; dates are not given. Interest is 10% p.a. Interest on drawings:
quiz.explain: When dates are unknown, assume drawings were spread evenly and charge for 6 months.
steps: Given: drawings ₹48,000, dates not given, 10% p.a.
Dates not given → charge for 6 months.
quiz.mistake: Charges interest for the full 12 months

quiz.q: The deed says interest on drawings is to be charged at a flat 5% (not per annum). A partner drew ₹40,000 at various times. Interest on drawings:
quiz.explain: A flat rate ignores time, so interest = 40,000 × 5% = ₹2,000.
steps: Given: flat 5% (not per annum) on drawings of ₹40,000.
quiz.mistake: Applies the 6-month average to a flat rate

quiz.q: A partner draws ₹4,000 in the middle of every month for the year. Interest is 12% p.a. Interest on drawings:
quiz.explain: Middle of each month → average 6 months: 48,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹2,880.
quiz.mistake: Uses 6.5 or 5.5 months instead of 6

teach.ask: Gappu took out money on different dates. Explain how interest on drawings is worked out.
teach.praise: Excellent! Products for different dates, 6.5/6/5.5 for monthly drawings, and 6 months when dates are unknown.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: if he draws the same amount at the start of every month, for how many months on average is interest charged?

revise.summary: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed provides it, for the time money is out of the business. Use the product method for different dates, average periods for equal drawings, 6 months when dates are unknown, and ignore time for a flat rate.
focus: The product method
Average periods for monthly and quarterly drawings
Dates not given and flat-rate cases
remember: Monthly: beginning 6.5, middle 6, end 5.5 months
Quarterly: beginning 7.5, middle 6, end 4.5 months
Dates not given: 6 months
Product method: total products × rate/100 × 1/12
traps: Don't apply time when the rate is flat (not per annum)
End-of-quarter average is 4.5, not 7.5, months
Count months till the year end, not from the year start

topics.title: Guarantee of profit to a partner

learn.hook: A star player joins a team only if promised a minimum fee. Firms do the same for a key partner – a guaranteed minimum profit.
points: A guarantee of profit assures a partner a minimum amount of profit. If his actual share is less, the shortfall (deficiency) is made good by the other partner(s).
Guarantee by the firm: the deficiency is borne by all the other partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
Guarantee by a particular partner: that partner alone bears the deficiency.
Guarantee by some partners in an agreed ratio: the deficiency is borne in that agreed ratio.
If the partner's actual share is equal to or more than the guaranteed amount, no adjustment is needed.

example.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C is guaranteed ₹60,000 by the firm. Profit is ₹3,00,000. Distribute it.
steps: A and B bear it 3:2: A ₹6,000, B ₹4,000.

learn.reallife: Start-ups that bring in an experienced CFO as a partner often promise a minimum yearly profit share to attract them, just as franchises guarantee fees to star cricketers.

games.title: Solving a guarantee question
items: Find the profit available for distribution
Compute the guaranteed partner's share in the profit-sharing ratio
Compare it with the guaranteed amount
Find the deficiency
Charge the deficiency to the guarantor partner(s) in the agreed ratio

games.title: Guarantee check
items: If the guarantee is given by the firm, the deficiency is borne by the other partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
All other partners share it in their mutual ratio.
A guaranteed partner can receive less than the guaranteed amount.
He always gets at least the guaranteed amount.
If the actual share exceeds the guaranteed amount, the partner gets the actual share.
The guarantee is a minimum, not a fixed amount.
When one partner gives the guarantee, the deficiency is shared by all partners.
Only the partner who gave the guarantee bears it.
The entry for deficiency borne by A in favour of C is Dr A's Capital A/c, Cr C's Capital A/c.
A's share falls and C's rises.

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C is guaranteed ₹60,000 by the firm. Profit is ₹3,00,000. A's final share:
quiz.explain: Deficiency ₹10,000 is borne by A and B in 3:2; A bears ₹6,000.
quiz.mistake: Makes A bear the whole deficiency

quiz.q: Same firm (3:2:1, profit ₹3,00,000), but only A guarantees C's ₹60,000. A's final share:
quiz.explain: A alone bears the ₹10,000 deficiency: 1,50,000 − 10,000 = ₹1,40,000.
quiz.mistake: Shares the deficiency between A and B though only A gave the guarantee

quiz.q: Same firm, but A and B bear C's deficiency equally. B's final share:
quiz.mistake: Uses the profit-sharing ratio instead of the agreed equal ratio

quiz.q: Same firm (3:2:1), C guaranteed ₹60,000, but profit is ₹4,20,000. C receives:
quiz.explain: C's actual share 4,20,000 × 1/6 = ₹70,000 exceeds the guarantee, so he takes ₹70,000.
steps: C keeps his actual share of ₹70,000.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the guaranteed amount is a fixed payment

quiz.q: P, Q and R share 2:2:1. R is guaranteed ₹50,000; P and Q bear any deficiency equally. Profit is ₹1,20,000. P's final share:
quiz.explain: R's share ₹24,000; deficiency ₹26,000 borne equally, so P bears ₹13,000: 48,000 − 13,000 = ₹35,000.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to deduct P's part of the deficiency

quiz.q: A guarantee of profit to a partner means:
options: the partner gets exactly the guaranteed amount every year
the partner gets at least the guaranteed amount; any shortfall is met by the guarantor(s)
the firm must always earn a fixed profit
the partner does not share losses of the firm
quiz.explain: It is a minimum. If the actual share is higher, the partner keeps the higher amount.
steps: A guarantee is a minimum amount.
If the actual share is less, the guarantor(s) make up the shortfall; if more, the partner keeps it.
Answer: the partner gets at least the guaranteed amount; any shortfall is met by the guarantor(s)
quiz.mistake: Treats the guarantee as a fixed salary

quiz.q: The firm (not any one partner) has guaranteed a minimum profit to D. The deficiency is borne by:
options: the partner with the largest capital
all other partners in their profit-sharing ratio
quiz.explain: A guarantee by the firm means the remaining partners share the deficiency in their own ratio.
steps: The deficiency is borne by all the other partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
Answer: all other partners in their profit-sharing ratio
quiz.mistake: Thinks the guaranteed partner shares his own deficiency

quiz.q: C's guaranteed profit is short by ₹8,000, and A alone has to make it good. The journal entry is:
options: Dr C's Capital A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹8,000
Dr Profit and Loss A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹8,000
Dr Cash A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹8,000
Dr A's Capital A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹8,000
quiz.explain: A gives up ₹8,000 of his share, which goes to C.
steps: A alone makes good C's ₹8,000 deficiency.
A gives up ₹8,000 and C receives it.
Entry: Dr A's Capital A/c, Cr C's Capital A/c ₹8,000.
Answer: Dr A's Capital A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹8,000
quiz.mistake: Reverses the debit and credit

teach.ask: Gappu was promised a minimum profit by his firm. Explain how the deficiency is handled.
teach.praise: Fantastic! Find the deficiency and charge it to whoever gave the guarantee, in the agreed ratio.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: who pays the shortfall if the firm itself gave the guarantee?

revise.summary: A guarantee of profit assures a partner a minimum share. Any deficiency is borne by other partners in their ratio (guarantee by the firm), by one partner alone, or in an agreed ratio. No adjustment is needed if the actual share is higher.
focus: Calculating the deficiency
Who bears it: firm, one partner or agreed ratio
Journal entry for the deficiency
remember: Deficiency = guaranteed amount − actual share
Guarantee by firm: other partners in their profit ratio
Entry: Dr guarantor's Capital A/c, Cr guaranteed partner's Capital A/c
traps: No adjustment if the actual share is more than the guarantee
The guaranteed partner does not bear his own deficiency
Debit the guarantor, not the guaranteed partner

learn.hook: Accounts closed, profits shared – and then someone notices interest on capital was forgotten. Do we reopen everything? No – one smart entry fixes it.
points: Past adjustments are needed when items such as interest on capital, interest on drawings or salary were omitted or wrongly given after the accounts were closed, or profit was shared in a wrong ratio.
Prepare a statement: (1) credit what each partner should have got, (2) debit what should have been charged, (3) reverse the wrong profit share and redistribute it correctly, (4) find the net effect.
The net effects add up to zero, because the firm's total profit does not change.
Pass one adjusting entry: Dr the partner(s) with net excess received / Cr the partner(s) with net shortfall. With fixed capitals, use current accounts.
For a wrong ratio, the net effect is simply (correct share − share actually given) for each partner.

example.q: A and B have capitals of ₹3,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. Profit of ₹80,000 was shared equally, but interest on capital at 10% p.a. was omitted. Pass the adjusting entry.
steps: This ₹40,000 should have reduced profit shared equally: debit each ₹20,000.
example.answer: Dr B's Capital A/c ₹10,000 / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000

learn.reallife: Just as Indian Railways issues a refund instead of re-running a train, accountants fix past errors with a single correcting entry instead of redoing the year's accounts.

items.text: Past adjustments are passed through partners' ___ accounts (current accounts if capitals are fixed).
The total of net effects of a past adjustment on all partners is ___.
A partner who received less than due is ___ in the adjusting entry.
For a wrong ratio, net effect = correct share − share actually ___.

games.title: Past adjustment facts
items: The total of net effects on all partners in a past adjustment is zero.
Only the division of profit changes, not the total.
Past adjustments require reopening the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
A single adjusting entry through capital/current accounts is enough.
With fixed capitals, past adjustments are passed through partners' current accounts.
Fixed capital accounts are not disturbed.
If profit was shared equally instead of 3:1, the partner with the larger correct share is debited.
He received less than due, so he is credited.
Omitted interest on drawings means partners with drawings were over-paid.
They should have been charged interest, so they are debited in the adjustment.

quiz.q: A (capital ₹3,00,000) and B (capital ₹1,00,000) shared ₹80,000 profit equally, omitting 10% interest on capital. Net effect on A:
quiz.explain: A should get ₹30,000 interest but bears half of the ₹40,000 total, a net gain of ₹10,000.
quiz.mistake: Credits A with the full interest without reducing his profit share

quiz.q: For the case above, the adjusting entry is:
options: Dr A's Capital A/c / Cr B's Capital A/c ₹10,000
Dr B's Capital A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000
Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹30,000
Dr Interest on Capital A/c / Cr A's and B's Capital A/cs ₹40,000
quiz.explain: B received ₹10,000 too much and A ₹10,000 too little, so B is debited and A credited.
steps: Interest omitted: A ₹30,000, B ₹10,000; this ₹40,000 would have cut profit shared equally (₹20,000 each).
B got ₹10,000 too much, A too little: Dr B's Capital A/c, Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000.
Answer: Dr B's Capital A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000
quiz.mistake: Reverses the debit and credit

quiz.q: Profit of ₹1,20,000 was shared equally between X and Y instead of 3:1. The adjusting entry amount is:
quiz.explain: X should get ₹90,000 but got ₹60,000; Y should get ₹30,000 but got ₹60,000. The transfer is ₹30,000 from Y to X.
quiz.mistake: Uses X's full correct share as the adjustment

quiz.q: A and B share equally. Interest on drawings was omitted: A ₹2,000 and B ₹1,000. In the adjusting entry, A's account will be debited by:
quiz.explain: Charge A ₹2,000 and B ₹1,000; credit the ₹3,000 back equally (₹1,500 each). Net: A −₹500, B +₹500.
quiz.mistake: Debits A with the full interest without crediting his half of the total

quiz.q: A and B share 2:1. Salary of ₹12,000 to B was omitted. The adjusting entry amount (Dr A, Cr B) is:
quiz.explain: B gets ₹12,000 but bears 1/3 of it (₹4,000) through reduced profit; A bears 2/3 = ₹8,000.
quiz.mistake: Transfers the full salary from A to B

quiz.q: Why are past errors in partners' accounts corrected by an adjusting entry rather than by redoing the accounts?
options: Because the firm's total profit has changed
The accounts are already closed; one entry changes only how profit was shared, which is all that went wrong
Because the Profit and Loss Account must be reprepared
quiz.explain: Total profit is unaffected; only partners' shares need correction, so one entry is enough.
steps: The accounts are already closed and total profit is unchanged.
So one adjusting entry is enough.
Answer: The accounts are already closed; one entry changes only how profit was shared, which is all that went wrong
quiz.mistake: Thinks the firm's profit changes after a past adjustment

quiz.q: In a past-adjustment statement, the sum of the net effects on all partners is:
options: equal to the difference in capitals
quiz.explain: Every rupee credited to one partner is debited to another; the firm's profit is unchanged.
steps: Every rupee credited to one partner is debited to another.
The firm's total profit is unchanged.
So the net effects add up to zero.
quiz.mistake: Expects the omitted amount to appear as a net figure

quiz.q: Partners' capitals are fixed. A past adjustment must be recorded through:
quiz.explain: With fixed capitals, all such adjustments go through current accounts.
steps: With fixed capitals, adjustments go through current accounts, not capital accounts.
quiz.mistake: Disturbs fixed capital accounts

teach.ask: Gappu forgot to give interest on capital after closing his books. Explain how to fix it.
teach.praise: Perfect! Find each partner's net effect and pass one adjusting entry – no need to reopen the books.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: after finding who gained and who lost, what entry does he pass?

revise.summary: Past adjustments correct omitted or wrong items after accounts are closed. A statement shows what each partner should have got, the net effect (totalling zero) is found, and one entry debits partners who got too much and credits those who got too little.
focus: Preparing the past-adjustment statement
Finding each partner's net effect
Passing the single adjusting entry
remember: Net effects of all partners total zero
Entry: Dr partner with net excess, Cr partner with net shortfall
Fixed capitals → use current accounts
traps: Don't redo the Profit and Loss Account; total profit does not change
Debit the partner who received too much
With fixed capitals, don't use capital accounts
